As each generation passes through a language model, information degrades monotonically per the Data Processing Inequality, yet no existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a document has undergone. We introduce the first systematic framework for generational depth estimation, combining a 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline—capturing surprisal dynamics, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics—with an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier that respects the ordinal structure of depth. We empirically measure the discrimination boundary K*, defined as the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain statistically distinguishable. Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total) at the ≤1.5B parameter scale, we find K*=2 is consistent: for the four model-mode configurations, bootstrap 95% CI lower bounds for 1-vs-2 all exceed θ=0.60 while all 2-vs-3 CI upper bounds fall below it; the four decoding strategies likewise yield point-estimate AUC above θ at 1-vs-2 and below at 2-vs-3. Cross-model transfer experiments show classifiers trained on one generator retain 80–92% accuracy on others, with binary (0-vs-1) transfer AUC exceeding 0.96 universally, indicating that depth features are largely text-intrinsic rather than generator-specific. Preliminary neural probing on one dataset yields K*_neural=3, suggesting our 15-feature K*=2 is a representation-dependent lower bound. Frontier LLMs achieve ~88% binary detection but only ~33% five-class depth accuracy—below our OBD classifier's 38.6%—confirming depth estimation as a non-trivial task requiring specialized features. Our findings motivate a three-tier taxonomy (human / generation-1 / generation-2+) for depth-aware data curation; we investigate whether this coarse ordinal signal enables graduated filtering that outperforms binary approaches discarding all synthetic content indiscriminately.
